From the root of your moos-ivp tree:

chatgpt.bodyTail:
rom my terminal. What should I check about the build, shell environment, PATH, and where the binaries are installed?

I’ll treat this as a terminal/build-path debugging checklist: first confirm the binaries exist, then confirm your shell is sourcing the right environment, then make the PATH change permanent.

Thought for 4s

This usually means MOOS-IvP compiled, but your terminal cannot see the installed executables. Check in this order.

1. Confirm the binaries were actually built

From the root of your moos-ivp tree:

Bash
cd ~/moos-ivp
find . -type f \( -name pAntler -o -name uXMS -o -name pMarineViewer \)

You should see paths like:

Bash
./bin/pAntler
./bin/uXMS
./bin/pMarineViewer

or possibly under a build/install directory depending on how you built it.

Also run:

Bash
ls -l ~/moos-ivp/bin | grep -E 'pAntler|uXMS|pMarineViewer'

If pAntler and uXMS exist but pMarineViewer does not, that often means the non-GUI MOOS tools built, but FLTK/OpenGL GUI dependencies were missing, so pMarineViewer did not compile. The official docs describe uXMS as a command-line MOOSDB scope tool, while pMarineViewer is an FLTK/OpenGL GUI app, so it has extra graphics dependencies. 
oceanai.mit.edu
+1

2. Run the build checker

MOOS-IvP includes a build-check.sh script that reports missing MOOS/IvP apps and libraries:

Bash
cd ~/moos-ivp
./build-check.sh

For a terse version:

Bash
./build-check.sh --terse

This is useful because “build completed” can still mean “some optional apps failed,” especially GUI tools. The script explicitly checks missing MOOS apps, IvP apps, MOOS libs, and IvP libs. 
GitHub

3. Check whether your shell can see them

Try:

Bash
which pAntler
which uXMS
which pMarineViewer

or:

Bash
command -v pAntler
command -v uXMS
command -v pMarineViewer

If those return nothing, your PATH does not include the MOOS-IvP bin directory.

You can still test the binary directly:

Bash
~/moos-ivp/bin/pAntler --help
~/moos-ivp/bin/uXMS --help
~/moos-ivp/bin/pMarineViewer --help

If direct execution works, the build is fine and this is purely a PATH issue.

4. Add MOOS-IvP binaries to PATH for the current terminal

Run:

Bash
export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/moos-ivp/bin

Then test:

Bash
which pAntler
which uXMS
which pMarineViewer

The MOOS-IvP extend documentation gives the same general instruction: after building, add the relevant bin directory to your shell path so apps can be launched normally, including through pAntler. 
oceanai.mit.edu

5. Make the PATH change permanent

First check your shell:

Bash
echo $SHELL

If it says zsh, edit ~/.zshrc:

Bash
echo 'export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/moos-ivp/bin' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

If it says bash, edit ~/.bashrc:

Bash
echo 'export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/moos-ivp/bin' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

On some Linux login shells, you may also need ~/.profile or ~/.bash_profile, but for normal terminal use ~/.bashrc/~/.zshrc is usually the right place.

6. Check for shell hash caching

Sometimes the shell remembers old command locations. After editing PATH, run:

Bash
hash -r

Then retry:

Bash
pAntler --help
uXMS --help
pMarineViewer --help
7. If using moos-ivp-extend, add that bin too

If you also built an extend tree, add both:

Bash
export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/moos-ivp/bin:$HOME/moos-ivp-extend/bin

Permanent version:

Bash
echo 'export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/moos-ivp/bin:$HOME/moos-ivp-extend/bin' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

Use ~/.bashrc instead if your shell is bash.

The extend tree docs specifically say its executables land in moos-ivp-extend/bin/, and that this directory should be added to PATH. 
oceanai.mit.edu

8. Check the common “wrong terminal / wrong environment” issue

Run:

Bash
echo $PATH
pwd
ls ~/moos-ivp/bin

Common mistakes:

Bash
# You built here:
~/Documents/moos-ivp

# But added this to PATH:
~/moos-ivp/bin

or:

Bash
# You added PATH in macOS terminal,
# but are now inside WSL, Docker, SSH, or another shell.

Each environment needs its own PATH setup.

9. Minimal known-good setup block

For your case, this is probably the block you want in ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc:

Bash
# MOOS-IvP
export MOOSIVP_HOME=$HOME/moos-ivp
export PATH=$PATH:$MOOSIVP_HOME/bin

# Optional extend tree
export MOOSIVP_EXTEND_HOME=$HOME/moos-ivp-extend
export PATH=$PATH:$MOOSIVP_EXTEND_HOME/bin

Then:

Bash
source ~/.zshrc   # or source ~/.bashrc
hash -r
which pAntler uXMS pMarineViewer
Likely diagnosis

If ~/moos-ivp/bin/pAntler works but pAntler does not, your build is fine; your PATH is missing ~/moos-ivp/bin.

If pAntler and uXMS exist but pMarineViewer does not, your core build likely succeeded but the GUI app did not build, usually because FLTK/OpenGL-related dependencies were missing.

chatgpt.title: MOOS-IvP Build Troubleshooting

assistant.text:
Here's a systematic checklist to diagnose why the MOOS-IvP binaries aren't on your PATH:

1. Confirm the binaries actually exist

First, check whether the build produced any executables at all:

bash

These are solid MOOS-IvP debugging questions. I'll work through them — let me know if you want any expanded into a deeper dive.

C03 — uXMS/uPokeDB Confusion
Check the MOOSDB is actually running. uPok

claude.bodyTail:
ty name mismatch — the shoreside pMarineViewer identifies vehicles by community/node name. If the missing vehicle's community name is wrong or duplicated, its reports may overwrite or be ignored.
Shoreside subscription — confirm the shoreside MOOSDB is receiving the NODE_REPORT (use uXMS on the shoreside community).
C12 — pShare Route Confusion

Mental model: each variable lives in the community where it was posted. pShare routes explicitly bridge communities.

Vehicle → Shoreside (typical): NODE_REPORT, NODE_MESSAGE, sensor summary variables.

Shoreside → Vehicle (typical): DEPLOY, MOOS_MANUAL_OVERRIDE, mission commands, VISIT_POINT assignments.

Stays local: NAV_X/Y/HEADING/SPEED, helm internals, DESIRED_HEADING/SPEED, behavior state — these are local control-loop variables that shoreside doesn't need and shouldn't overwrite.

A common mistake is sharing too little (missing NODE_REPORT) or too much (accidentally sharing DEPLOY back to itself, causing loops).

C13 — TSP App / Behavior Boundary

Clear division of responsibility:

Your MOOS app computes the ordered waypoint list and posts it as an updates string to the helm, e.g.: Notify("SURVEY_UPDATES", "points=10,20:30,40:50,60").
BHV_Waypoint receives that update string via its updates parameter in the .bhv file: updates = SURVEY_UPDATES.
The helm reads the update on the next iterate cycle and reconfigures BHV_Waypoint's point list.

If the vehicle doesn't follow the path: confirm the updates variable name matches exactly, confirm BHV_Waypoint is in a running (not idle/completed) state in uHelmScope, and confirm the condition for BHV_Waypoint is satisfied.

C14 — Distributed Route Assignment
Vehicle identity — each vehicle must know its own name (usually from the community name or a VNAME variable). If two vehicles share a name or a vehicle reads the wrong assignment, one gets both routes.
Assignment message format — confirm the variable name, destination field, and payload format all match what the receiving vehicle's app expects.
Timing — if assignments are sent before the receiving vehicle's app is registered, the message is dropped. Use uTimerScript delays or condition the assignment on a vehicle-ready variable.
Activation condition — BHV_Waypoint won't start until its condition (e.g. DEPLOY == true AND ASSIGNED == true) is satisfied. Confirm the assignment variable is reaching the vehicle and is spelled correctly.
C15 — Multi-Machine Networking
IP addresses — in pShare routes, localhost only works when both communities are on the same machine. Use explicit IPs for cross-machine routing.
MOOSDB ServerHost — on each machine, the MOOSDB must bind to the machine's actual IP (or 0.0.0.0), not just localhost.
Firewall / UFW — MOOS ports (typically 9000-range) and pShare ports must be open on both machines. Test with nc -zv <ip> <port>.
Launch timing — the shoreside MOOSDB must be up before vehicles try to connect via pShare. Add a delay in vehicle launch scripts when on separate machines.
Clock sync — MOOS timestamps can cause issues if machines' clocks diverge significantly. Use NTP.
C16 — Message Does Not Arrive

The path for NODE_MESSAGE_LOCAL:

Your app posts NODE_MESSAGE_LOCAL locally.
uFldNodeComms (on shoreside) or uFldMessageHandler receives it, processes destination routing, and re-posts the payload variable to the destination vehicle's community via pShare.
The payload variable appears in the destination vehicle's MOOSDB.

Check: Is uFldNodeComms actually running on shoreside? Is the src_node name recognized (does it match the vehicle's community name)? Is dest_node spelled correctly? Is pShare carrying the result back to the destination vehicle?

C17 — Node Names / Destinations
src_node must match the community name of the sending vehicle exactly — this is how the broker knows who sent it.
dest_node must match the community name of the receiving vehicle exactly — a single character difference means no delivery.
Use uXMS on the shoreside to see if NODE_MESSAGE is arriving there, then check if the broker is re-posting the payload. This isolates whether the problem is in the send, the broker, or the final delivery.
C18 — Behavior Never Runs
condition = — use uHelmScope to see why the behavior is idle. It shows which conditions are unsatisfied.
pwt (priority weight) — if pwt = 0, the behavior participates in the IvP solve but with zero weight, producing no effect.
InfoBuffer — the behavior's onRunState() r

Claude works directly with your codebase

Let Claude edit files, run commands, and ship changes from the desktop app, your terminal, or your IDE.

Install

PASTED





